newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: U.S. says has not taken action against Petronas.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says has not taken action against Petronas.

text.p: The U.S. embassy in Malaysia said on Friday that the United States has not taken or recommended any action against Malaysian state oil firm Petronas over its involvement in projects in Iran.

In a statement, the U.S. embassy said: "Media reports that a U.S. government 'sanctions committee' responsible for implementing the Iran-Libya Sanctions Act has recommended actions against Petronas in accordance with the bill are false."
Reports that the U.S. might impose sanctions against Petronas had weakened the ringgit this week.
The statement said: "No 'sanctions committee' has been established, and the U.S. government has not taken or recommended any action against Petronas."
On Tuesday, a legislative aide to U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato -- the sanctions law's major congressional sponsor -- said the U.S. might consider taking action against Petronas.

Referring to the aide's comments, the U.S. embassy statement said: "These media reports refer to a statement by a Congressional aide, who expressed his own views. The aide does not speak for or represent the policy or views of the U.S. government."

U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said in New York on the same day that the Clinton administration would wait until after the U.S. presidential elections on November 5 to decide on how it will enforce its sanctions law against Libya and Iran.

The reports, as well as talk that Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara, was comfortable with the ringgit at the 2.53 level, triggered ringgit sales on Wednesday, foreign exchange dealers said. The Malaysian currency fell to a six-month low on that day and closed at 2.5250/60.
Petronas holds a 30 percent stake in Iran's Sirri oilfields exploration project, which also involves French company Total SA .
The investment in the $600 million project puts Petronas over the $40 million a year level that the U.S. has said non-U.S. firms can invest in Iran and Libya's oil and gas sectors.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Thursday his country intends to proceed with the investment, despite the threats of U.S. sanctions.
